kessef_hakodashim.en: Seif 2. For preserves and the like, that all of it be sound. Concerning a kind of salt known as talfin, softness that makes it unable to keep may constitute a defect. Since a retail seller must expect the purchaser to store the goods for some time, this may be comparable to one who says that he needs produce for preserving. The matter must be evaluated according to commercial practice. If the purchaser is uncertain whether the defect existed before the sale and suggests that the problem may have arisen because the product had not yet completed its manufacturing process, no special presumption may resolve the issue. The burden remains on the claimant, and the seller can say, 'I do not know whether I ever became obligated.' Even if the uncertainty is more like 'I do not know whether I repaid,' in light of the Taz's discussion of a counterfeit coin one may still say that the seller had no reason to know the item's exact condition while it was in his possession. I encountered such a case with salt that had been moist and soft. It was uncertain whether it softened only after the purchaser acquired it, while being transported through snow and frost, or whether it had already been soft before final drying by the fire. The allocation of the burden of proof depends on these circumstances.

kessef_hakodashim.en: Seif 9. Before it reached there the price fell, see the Tur. The Tur in siman 230 cites Rabbeinu Chananel and the Ramah that where no money had yet been paid and the purchaser disclosed that he was buying wine in order to take it to a place where it was dearer, he may withdraw when that purpose fails. One should not automatically extend that ruling to a case where transportation costs later rose because the roads deteriorated, or where transport later became impossible. We should not multiply disputes unnecessarily, and perhaps everyone agrees that because disclosed intent ordinarily has no effect in movables, as in siman 207, the buyer's statement that he was purchasing specifically to transport the goods does not itself create a condition. According to Shaarei Ephraim, however, a possessor may say kim li like the Ramah's view in the Tur that disclosed intent can be effective even for movables. On that approach, perhaps the onaah calculation might follow the market at the destination to which the buyer expressly said he was taking the goods, because the purchase was made for that place. Possibly, if the disclosed intent came from the seller, only the seller may invoke it, and if it came from the buyer, only the buyer may do so. Yet reason suggests that disclosed intent should not determine onaah at all. Every merchant who buys for resale intends to profit, and everyone knows he does not buy in order to lose money. If such intent controlled onaah, even a tiny loss to a reseller who stated his purpose should void the sale, and no authority has ruled so. Perhaps disclosed intent works only when a person sells something not ordinarily intended for sale, or where it concerns the essential character and grade of the object. Profit and loss, however, are commercial risks every buyer and seller accepts. Therefore, for onaah, all may agree that valuation follows only the actual place and time of the transaction, and a stated intention to transport elsewhere does not alter it. This still requires careful study.

And it turned sour within three days. The Mechaber abbreviated Rambam's language. The Tur states more fully: if it turns sour within three days, the loss is the seller's, and even if the seller already received the money he must return it. Since it was found to be vinegar within three days, it certainly had already begun to turn sour earlier. Although wine that smells like vinegar but tastes like wine is legally wine, a person does not pay the ordinary price for wine that has already begun the process that will spoil it. Even if the purchaser tasted it and both smell and taste seemed like wine, we say he did not taste it properly. If it turns sour after three days, the loss is the purchaser's, and even if he has not yet paid he must pay. Since he tasted it and it was good, the presumption is that the spoilage arose later. If he did not taste it, however, the burden of proof lies upon the claimant because the matter is doubtful. All this applies where he left it in the seller's vessels. In the Derishah I explained why this differs from an animal found with a perforation in the reticulum after three days, where at the end of siman 224 and in siman 232 the Tur and Mechaber place the loss upon the purchaser even if it is doubtful whether the defect arose with seller or purchaser, and even require an unpaid buyer to pay. Beer is naturally destined to sour if left standing, so we cannot place it under a strong presumption of remaining sound. An animal has a presumption of bodily health. At the end of this siman Rama repeats the present law concerning a purchased barrel of beer without adding anything new. Perhaps he did not notice that the Mechaber had already stated it, because he copied it from the Tur where it appears again. We find many such repetitions. It is nevertheless surprising that Rama does not reproduce all the Tur's details. This requires study.

Likewise, one who receives barrels of wine, etc. This is Rambam's language in chapter 17. It means that just as where one sells wine to another to resell little by little the risk may remain upon the seller, so too where one receives barrels from another to sell in a specified place, since the giver knew they would remain for some time and the price fell in the interim, the loss is the giver's. Yet the cases are not entirely identical. In the first clause the Mechaber speaks even of an outright sale. Here he says 'one who receives from another.' The Tur cites Rabbeinu Yonah and writes that specifically in such a receiving arrangement the risks of price decline and souring remain upon the owner. If he bought the wine outright, even if he said that he was buying it in order to transport it to a place where wine was expensive, a later decline in price is the purchaser's risk and he cannot retract. Rabbeinu Chananel disagrees and holds that even in an outright purchase he may retract in such a case. Ramah also agrees but distinguishes that this applies specifically when the purchaser has not yet paid and stated that he would not pay until he brought the wine to the destination. See the Tur and Maggid Mishneh for the variant readings and opinions.

netivot_hamishpat_beurim.en: Likewise one who receives barrels of wine. See Sema, seif katan 15. At first glance this law is very difficult. If the wine rises in value at the destination, the profit is divided. If one were to say that when it falls in price before arrival the depreciation is borne entirely by the investor, then the recipient would share in profit but not in loss. Yet they expressly agreed to share loss as well. It is strained to say that the recipient bears half the depreciation only when the wine initially rose in value at the destination, he failed to sell immediately, and it then fell. Daily commercial practice is plainly otherwise: one who receives an iska specifically to transport merchandise to a place shares the loss if the merchandise falls in price there. What basis would there be to give the recipient a stronger position than the investor, such that he shares the appreciation but not the depreciation? Siman 176, seif 40, in the gloss, says explicitly that merchandise is evaluated for appreciation and depreciation according to its market price when it is transported, implying that if the price falls after transport begins the loss is shared. All the more difficult is the view of Rabbeinu Chananel and Ramah cited by Sema, which would apply a similar rule even to an outright buyer, contrary to common commercial law. Tur states expressly that theft loss is shared, but does not explain who bears accidents. Shulchan Aruch omits the accident rule entirely. In my view Rama's rule in siman 176 comes from Mahari Weil cited by Beit Yosef, who says it is learned from the chapter HaMokher Et HaBayit and from this sugya. That indicates he understands the Gemara's phrase "before he brought it there, the price fell" as meaning before the recipient began transporting it to the cheap market. Nimukei Yosef likewise supports this reading. If the price falls after transport has begun, the loss is shared. Similarly, appreciation occurring before transport begins belongs to the investor, while appreciation after transport begins is shared. The reason is that before transport the recipient has not yet begun performing the enterprise and has not yet acquired a profit-bearing relation to the goods. Therefore, concerning depreciation he can say: since appreciation would still have been yours, the depreciation is likewise yours. This is the rule of siman 176. In our siman, however, the text follows Rashbam's interpretation, that the wine fell in price before arrival even though transport had already begun. Rashbam explains that the wine did not become cheaper only in the destination town, but across the entire region. This resolves the questions. If the wine falls only in the destination market, the recipient certainly shares the depreciation, because the entire transaction was expressly made on the understanding that profit and loss at that market would be divided. But if some general event causes wine prices to fall throughout the country, the investor alone bears the loss for a different reason. Tosafot in Ketubot 47 ask why in every purchase of an animal that later dies or becomes treifah we do not say the buyer never intended to purchase under such circumstances. They answer that where the matter depends on both parties, we do not infer such an unstated condition. Mishneh LaMelech questions this because in the case "he wrote for her only on condition that he marry her," both parties also have intent; likewise in a sale made because the seller needed money. He explains that where the inferred condition causes no real loss to the other party, we may apply the umdena. A widow whose husband dies simply returns to being unmarried; the husband has no posthumous loss from the condition. In a sale made only because the seller needed cash, if that need disappears, the buyer gets his money back and the seller gets his property back. By contrast, if a purchased cow later dies and the buyer recovers the price while the seller receives only a carcass or nothing, the inferred condition would impose a real loss on the seller. We therefore do not assume he agreed. This is analogous to Tosafot in Bava Kamma 110 concerning a woman who falls before a levir afflicted with boils. The husband's death does not create a conflicting interest for him after death. Even this explanation requires qualification. If one buys a house and later the king decrees that this buyer may no longer live in the city, why not say the buyer never intended the purchase under such circumstances, since the seller could simply take the house back and return the money? The answer is that Tosafot do not mean that every later catastrophe undoes a purchase before the buyer has actually used the item. Once the buyer has already received the very practical benefit for which he purchased, there is no such umdena. In marriage, Tosafot themselves distinguish that before full marriage there may be such a presumption, but after marriage there is not. The same applies to a cow or house. Once it became available for the intended use, even if the buyer had not yet actually used it, the acquisition benefit has already vested, like a bride entering chuppah and becoming fit for relations. Tosafot in Bava Metzia 79 similarly write regarding a specific ship that once payment was given the parties resolved that the money should belong immediately. Therefore Tosafot's original question concerns only a case where the cow died or became treifah immediately, before it became available for the purpose for which it was bought, such as where the parties had stipulated that it would remain in the seller's possession for a day or two before use. That resembles a betrothal that never reached marriage. Only there is their distinction needed: since the inferred condition would cause loss to the seller, we do not apply it. By contrast, if a house was purchased but was not yet available for use and, before it became available, a general event occurred that would clearly have prevented the buyer from purchasing had he known, the transaction can be void where returning the house and price leaves the seller without loss. This explains our case. A general event caused wine prices to fall throughout the whole country. This resembles a widespread catastrophe. The recipient plainly did not accept the iska on the understanding of bearing that kind of general market collapse. The investor suffers no special loss from recognizing the umdena, because he simply receives the same wine back and it would have depreciated even had it remained in his own house. Moreover, the event occurred before the recipient had become able to derive the intended commercial benefit from the iska. He was forbidden to sell the wine before reaching the destination. Therefore the umdena applies and the general depreciation falls on the investor alone. This also explains why in an outright sale the result differs. An outright buyer could ordinarily resell the wine immediately. From the moment of purchase the property was fully available for commercial benefit. Therefore the later regional fall in price does not undo his acquisition. But even in an iska, if the price falls only in the destination market, the recipient shares the loss because that is exactly the commercial risk the parties expressly agreed to divide. Even if one could formulate an umdena, the express condition controls.

siftei_kohen.en: Until Shavuot, etc. The Rama distinguishes the case specifically where the wine remains in the seller's cask. In my opinion the ruling follows the Ri cited by the Beit Yosef in seif 2, that even when the wine was transferred into the purchaser's casks, the seller must provide wine that will last until Shavuot. This is also the view of the Ran cited by the Beit Yosef in seif 1. The Ran writes that where the seller said, 'I am selling you fragrant wine,' this is the case taught in the Mishna, that he must provide wine lasting until Shavuot, even though it was poured into the purchaser's casks, for the latter clause is taught in a manner parallel to the first. I found this among writings from my youth.
